title: Polaroid and the Digital Camera
text:
Polaroid, founded by Edwin Land, built its fortune on instant photography: cameras that produced a finished print within minutes. Its business model, like that of many camera firms, relied on selling cameras at modest margins and earning profits on the film that customers bought again and again.

In 2000 Mary Tripsas and Giovanni Gavetti, then at Harvard Business School, published a detailed case study of how Polaroid responded to digital imaging from the early 1980s to the late 1990s. Based on company documents and interviews with managers and engineers, they showed that Polaroid was not slow to develop the technology. It invested heavily in digital imaging research and by the early 1990s had developed advanced image sensors and a high-resolution digital camera with strong technical performance.

The problem was not technical capability but the beliefs of senior managers. Leadership remained convinced that profits came from consumables, so a camera that needed no film was hard to fit into its plans. It also believed that customers would always want physical prints, and it judged new projects by whether they fit the instant photography business. Digital products were steered toward printing and toward markets that matched those assumptions. When digital cameras took off for consumers, Polaroid was not positioned to benefit.

Tripsas and Gavetti concluded that managers' mental models of how their business makes money can trap a company even when it holds the right technology. Polaroid filed for bankruptcy in 2001.
lesson: Owning a new capability is not enough if your beliefs about how you succeed stay the same. Regularly question the assumptions behind your business model, especially the ones that made you successful.
source: Tripsas, M., and Gavetti, G. (2000). Capabilities, cognition, and inertia: Evidence from digital imaging. Strategic Management Journal, 21(10-11), 1147-1161.
